keywords: burning rate model accuracy error RMSE Ridge CatBoost how good

statement: For flame extinction diameter, CatBoost has error (RMSE) 0.497 mm against 0.566 mm for Ridge and 1.037 mm for always guessing the mean.

statement: For burning rate, the inputs that matter most to the team's CatBoost model are oxygen fraction (error rises by 0.048 when shuffled), initial droplet diameter (error rises by 0.017 when shuffled), carbon dioxide fraction (error rises by 0.015 when shuffled); pressure matters little (error change 0.001).

statement: The refined extinction-diameter model (CatBoost with physics-based inputs, constrained to rise with initial droplet size) has error (RMSE) 0.487 mm against 0.497 mm before, and was better in 64% of held-out folds; its plus-or-minus 0.84 mm band covered 92% of runs on held-out test dates.
keywords: refined improved better extinction diameter model accuracy error RMSE uncertainty band range how sure confidence
method: grouped cross-validation, REPORT.md section 9

statement: A new model gives the chance a FLEX droplet breaks apart (disruption): on held-out test dates it ranks break-ups above other endings with AUC 0.86, and its average predicted chance matched the observed rate of 21% of runs. Asking whether a droplet breaks apart works better than the original three-way test-end model (balanced accuracy 0.77 against 0.58).
keywords: disruption break apart breaks up droplet model chance likely likelihood probability predict test end how runs ended accuracy
method: grouped cross-validation, REPORT.md section 9

statement: At Moon-Base-like conditions (30% oxygen, 527.5 mmHg, 2 mm droplet) the disruption model gives a 89% chance a methanol droplet breaks apart and 95% for heptane, in line with the data: 17 of 23 FLEX runs at 28% oxygen or more broke apart.
keywords: Moon base lunar 30% oxygen low pressure disruption break apart
method: disruption model prediction and FLEX outcome counts
caveat: Few runs exist at exactly these conditions: read it as a trend, not a measurement.

statement: Moon-Base conditions (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi = 527.5 mmHg) sit at the low-pressure edge of the FLEX data: only 9 methanol and 7 heptane runs have oxygen of 30% or more at 620 mmHg or less, so the extinction-diameter and test-end models are not valid there.
keywords: Moon base lunar habitat valid validity predictions 30% oxygen low pressure 10.2 psi extrapolation coverage
method: coverage counts from results.json
caveat: No measured partial-gravity data exists in PSI; these are microgravity tables.

statement: FLEX droplets burn well below the textbook (classical droplet-combustion theory) burning rate: the median run reaches about 0.67 of the textbook value for methanol and 0.35 for heptane (257 runs).
keywords: textbook theory classical droplet combustion theory d2 law predicted expected measured compare slower than theory physics gap ratio
method: measured burning rate divided by the theory value per run, median per fuel (07_physics_check.py)
caveat: The textbook formula leaves out radiation heat loss, soot and unsteady effects, and the team's gas property values are rough: trust the direction and rough size, not the exact ratios.

statement: Adding the textbook burning-rate value to the team's Ridge model barely changes its error on held-out test days (0.0735 against 0.0736 mm2/s); the textbook value alone, even scaled per fuel, does worse (0.185) than always guessing the mean (0.138).
keywords: physics theory hybrid physics-informed model improve accuracy error textbook add help better
method: grouped cross-validation on whole test dates, same folds as the other models

statement: On every FLEX run, the team's burning-rate model moves the same way as textbook theory when a gas replaces nitrogen: more oxygen and more helium make droplets burn faster, more carbon dioxide makes them burn slower.
keywords: physics theory agree consistent direction oxygen helium carbon dioxide CO2 burning rate faster slower model sanity check
method: sign of the change in the Ridge prediction and in the theory value, per run (07_physics_check.py)

statement: A textbook buoyancy estimate, not a measurement, says a 2 mm droplet in air at sea-level pressure would burn about 1.5 times as fast on Earth, 1.4 times on Mars and 1.3 times on the Moon as on the ISS; in Moon Base air (30% oxygen, 527.5 mmHg) the Moon factor is about 1.3.
keywords: Moon lunar Mars Earth gravity partial gravity buoyancy faster burn burning rate estimate theory scaling Grashof convection
method: natural-convection correlation Nu = 2 + 0.6 Gr^(1/4) Pr^(1/3) with rough gas properties (physics.py)
caveat: No partial-gravity droplet data exists in PSI to check this against.
